The proposed solutions for both segments had higher costs than alternatives but were selected based on the projects’ benefits including increased transfer capacity, deferred transmission upgrades, greater operational flexibility, and more resilient structure design. The PPTPP allows the NYPSC and project developers opportunities to develop a project-specific cost allocation but retains a backstop cost allocation method based on load ratio share to prevent project delays in cases in which an alternative agreement cannot be reached. For the AC Transmission Needs study, the NYPSC recommended the NYISO adopt an alternative cost allocation scheme in its December 2015 order (State of New York Public Service Commission Order Finding Transmission Needs Driven by Public Policy Requirements 2015). The adjusted method assigns 75% of costs to load zones based on reduced energy payments estimated over a 10-year period and 25% of costs to all load zones in the New York Control Area based on load ratio share of the forecasted summer peak demand. The adopted approach allows for more granular cost allocation to load downstate, which bears the largest cost responsibility. C.3 SPP Priority Projects SPP’s Priority Projects originated in 2009 from a short-term working group called the Synergistic Planning Project Team (SPPT) created to review transmission planning processes and cost allocation methodologies and to provide recommendations to SPP (SPP 2009). The 17 Section 31.4.8.1 in Attachment Y of the NYISO’s OATT and the Public Policy Transmission Planning Manual defines some of the benefits metrics used to evaluate potential projects against: capital costs, cost-per-megawatt ratio, impact of proposed project on future construction (expandability), operational flexibility, operational performance (utilization, power flows), developer access to property rights, and any other metrics defined by the NYPSC (NYISO 2020). In addition to the transfer capacity minimum thresholds, the NYPSC, in its December 2015 Order, defined other criteria for the NYISO to include in its evaluation of potential solutions. For example, any solution must have access to existing right-of-way, minimize the acquisition of property rights, cannot cross the Hudson River, and the NYISO should favor solutions that replace aging infrastructure. 58 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. SPPT comprised state regulators from the regional state committee (RSC), SPP members, representatives of SPP, an independent external stakeholder, and a facilitator. In its final report to the SPP Board, the SPPT recommended SPP identify a portfolio of “Priority Projects” to recommend to the RSC (SPP 2009). The Priority Projects portfolio consisted of upgraded transmission facilities that past transmission planning studies had previously identified as solutions, including the numerous extra-high-voltage overlay studies to address network congestion, connect new generation resources, and improve connectivity between the east and west portions of the SPP footprint.18 In April 2010, the SPP Board of Directors approved a portfolio of five Priority Projects, and the projects were built in 2017.
